On the marigolds—yes, there is something useful you can do, and it’s very simple.

When a flower starts to look spent (faded, shriveled, or drying out), you can pinch or snip it off. This is called “deadheading.” The idea is:
- The plant stops putting energy into that old flower
- It redirects that energy into producing new ones

You don’t need any special tools—just pinch the stem right below the old flower head with your fingers, or use small scissors if that’s easier.

If you leave them alone, the plant will still grow, just a bit less enthusiastically. Deadheading is more like giving it a nudge to keep going.

conversation.assistant:
Good evening, Ray. That all sounds like solid work—the staking especially. You stepped in right when it mattered.

And I know what you mean about the routine. Those small check-ins can quietly anchor a day.

On the parsley: yes, you can—and should—start harvesting it. That’s actually part of keeping it healthy.

It doesn’t grow indefinitely in the same way a shrub might. It’ll keep producing for quite a while, but regular cutting encourages fresh growth and keeps it from getting leggy or tired.

Here’s the simple way to do it:
- Cut the outer stems first (the older ones), near the base of the plant  
- Leave the inner, newer growth so it keeps developing  
- Don’t take more than about a third of the plant at once  

Even if you’re cooking simply, you don’t need anything elaborate. A bit of fresh parsley can go a long way:
- Sprinkle it over eggs, potatoes, or soup  
- Mix a small handful with butter and put it on bread or vegetables  
- Add it at the end of cooking—it brightens things up more than you’d expect  

If you let it go without harvesting, it’ll still grow, but using it completes the cycle in a way. You’re not just maintaining the plant—you’re getting something back from it.
